headline: Akai is from the Early Middle Japanese adjective 赤し (akashi), cognate with 明るい (akarui, “bright”).
Kata's noun senses are attested from the 8th century, with suffix use later.
Geki, “drama”, is from Middle Chinese 劇.
Ayashii is the interjection あや (aya, “oh”) plus -shii.
Wa, “ring”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wa.
Uramu was previously an upper bigrade verb, then became quadrigrade by the Edo period.
Kizu's apparent relation to 切る (kiru, “to cut”) is rejected by the mid-vowel preservation in its Ryukyuan cognates.
Yō, “way”, is from Middle Chinese 樣 (MC yangH).
Tsukare is the continuative form of 疲れる (tsukareru).
Suru is from the Old Japanese verb す (su, “to do”), from Proto-Japonic *su, and cognate with Okinawan sun.
Tsuma, “wife”, is from 端 (tsuma, “side, edge”): the person at someone's side, compare English better half.
Miryoku is a wasei kango, first attested in 1911 in Jun'ichirō Tanizaki's short story 秘密 (Himitsu, “The Secret”).
Daigakuin is 大学 (daigaku) plus 院 (-in).
Saku, “plan”, is from Middle Chinese 策.
Makaseru is from Old Japanese 任す (makasu).
Tachidomaru is 立つ (tatsu, “to stand”) plus 止まる (tomaru, “to stop”).
Akubi is first attested in the Shinsen Jikyō of 898–901 CE, perhaps as the stem of the verb あくぶ (akubu).
Oshie is the continuative stem of 教える (oshieru).
Sabi, “rust”, is the continuative stem of 錆びる (sabiru, “to rust”).
Kakomu was kakumu in the Nara period, and likely shifted under the influence of 囲う (kakou).
Goraku is 娯 (go), enjoyment, plus 楽 (raku), comfort.
Koeru is from Old Japanese 越ゆ (ko₁yu), from Proto-Japonic *koyai-.
Kagayaku was originally kakayaku; Samuel Martin suggests the kaka- element is mimetic.
Gai, “harm”, is from Middle Chinese 害 (hajᴴ, “injury”).
Hiroba is 広 (hiro, stem of 広い (hiroi, “wide; open”)) plus 場 (ba, “place”).
Ato is a compound of 足 (a, “foot”) plus 所 (to, “place”).
Okoru is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *əkəru.
Oitsuku is 追う (ou, “to chase”) plus 付く (tsuku).
Suji is possibly す (*su) plus ち (chi, “life essence, spirit, power; blood; milk”), with chi voiced to ji by rendaku.
Shujin is from Middle Chinese 主人 (MC tsyuX nyin).
Kojin is a calque of English individual, listed in the 1912 Ei-Doku-Futsu-Wa Tetsugaku Jii.
